source.title: How does fine-tuning improve sensorimotor representations in large language models?
source.authors: Minghua Wu; Javier Conde; Pedro Reviriego; Marc Brysbaert

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses partial convergence between fine-tuned models, but its reported cross-model correlations concern word-level model-to-human similarity scores, not similarity between models’ representations of the same inputs as the claim specifies. It does not test convergence with scale or the listed versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-to-human RSA and rating results, but those compare each model with human ratings rather than measuring convergence between models. Its inter-model correlations are correlations between word-level model-to-human similarity scores; these are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version, not as tests of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes one base model (GPT-4o-mini) on human sensorimotor ratings and measures how closely its rating outputs match human norms. It does not compare representations of independently trained models, sweep scale, pair modalities, vary seeds, map between models or look for shared features. Its 'partial convergence' language refers to correlations between models' per-word model-human accuracy scores, which is a related but different construct. It does not cite the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Rating-based fine-tuning improves alignment with human sensorimotor norms through targeted reorganization rather than a global boost. It transfers robustly across English and Dutch and to untrained motor dimensions, but poorly from a QA task format. En_FT and Nl_FT show partial cross-lingual convergence.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes one base model on human sensorimotor ratings and evaluates model-human alignment; it does not apply the original cross-model convergence or scale-comparison method.
record.method_sensitivity: Fine-tuning objective and language affect the reported word-level score correlations: rating-tuned models are moderately correlated, base-to-rating-tuned rankings are near zero or negative, and QA_FT remains strongly correlated with Base but is reported as uncorrelated with the supervised models.

fits_no_version.finding: Two fine-tunes of the same base model on a shared rating objective in different languages show moderately correlated per-word accuracy rankings (ρ=.368). Base-to-rating-tuned rankings are near zero or negative. The QA-tuned model stays close to Base (ρ=.656).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A shared fine-tuning objective can align which concepts a model gets right across languages, while a different task format leaves the base model's pattern intact.

record.problems: Only one base model is studied, with no scale or model-capability sweep. The inter-model correlations are correlations of word-level model-human similarity scores rather than direct comparisons of model representational geometry.
record.rows_left_out: Model-human RSA, dimension-wise correlations, and concept-level accuracy results are not included as rows because they compare model predictions with human ratings, not convergence between models. Figure-only values are not extracted.

untested.parts: No scale or capability sweep. No independently trained models with different architectures, objectives or data.
No different-seed training and no shared-feature or subspace analysis.
No linear maps, stitching, relative representations or unpaired mapping.
No neuron, SAE feature or circuit analysis across models.
Multiple model-human metrics are used, but model-to-model convergence is never measured under varied metrics or inputs.
No direct model-model representational alignment, no plateau, and no test of shared data or objectives against a common model of reality.

record.verdict_notes: All 'representations' here are vectors of numeric ratings generated by prompting, not internal embeddings. RSA compares each model's output-rating RDM with the human RDM. Only one base model and its three fine-tunes are studied, so this is not evidence on any version of the convergence claim.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep, nor comparison of representations from independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No paired image-caption data or vision-language representation comparison.
No models trained from different initializations and no analysis of shared features, subspaces, units, or bases.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
The paper uses multiple measures of model-to-human alignment but does not test whether model-to-model convergence changes with similarity measure, settings, or input distribution.

The reported inter-model measure is correlation between word-level model-to-human similarity scores, not direct model-representation alignment. No plateau or comparison of shared training data/objectives against a common model of reality is tested.
